FIRE · 2025

On the Perils of Progress and the Unsolicited Gift of Superiority (A.K.A.,

6 October 2025·5 min read·928 words

Archived verbatim. Published 6 October 2025 on Medium, in the Fire era — before Brad Devices shipped anything. The prose is the record and is not edited here; corrections go in a new essay.

A treatise on how to gracefully accept a handout without losing your self-proclaimed god complex.

Ah, another glorious day in the relentless pursuit of technocratic overlordship. Another dawn breaks, finding The Architect, me, Festus Bradley Nyadimo, poised at the precipice of… well, a slightly less frustrating computing experience, it seems. Because, dear readers, it has come to pass: I am no longer operating on the digital equivalent of a wheelbarrow with one flat tire and a perpetually jammed axle. I have been gifted.
Yes, you heard that right. Gifted. The word itself, it chafes, doesn’t it? It rattles against the very foundations of my meticulously crafted ideology, an ideology forged in the white-hot crucible of the Kisian market, where every byte was earned, every pixel a hard-won trophy. My venerable A05—a device that was less a phone and more a philosophical statement on the merits of brutal self-reliance—was the very embodiment of my initial foray into digital dominion. It was tough. It was slow. It froze with the regularity of a government official’s promise. And it was mine, earned through the sweat of my brow and the cunning of a nascent entrepreneur.
I chronicled its genesis, its gritty ascent from mere silicon to a symbol of raw, unadulterated hustle. It taught me patience (mostly in waiting for apps to load), resilience (in not throwing it against a wall), and the profound wisdom that if you want something done, you do it yourself. It was the digital monk’s robe to my austere devotion to creation. It humbled me daily, reminding me that true power isn’t in the tools, but in the grit that overcomes their limitations. Or so I told myself, usually while staring at a frozen screen for the fifth time in an hour, wondering if my IDE had achieved sentience and was actively plotting against me.
But alas, the universe, in its infinite comedic wisdom, has decided to throw a wrench—a very shiny, efficient, and unexpectedly generous wrench—into my carefully constructed narrative. My mother, bless her discerning eye and uncanny ability to spot outright suffering disguised as stoic perseverance, observed my struggle. She witnessed the slow, agonizing death of productivity. She saw the "Architect" reduced to muttering curses at a perpetually buffering compile.
And so, like a benevolent goddess descending from Mount Olympus with a perfectly engineered lightning bolt, she presented me with… the Galaxy A16.
Initially, I scoffed. Internally, of course. My pride, that finely honed instrument of self-aggrandizement, bristled. A gift? For me? The man who built empires on sheer stubbornness? This felt like cheating. This felt like… privilege. The kind of soft, coddling indulgence I’d so vehemently railed against in my early philosophical treaties (which, incidentally, would have taken ten minutes to open on the A05).
But then… then I opened the damn thing.
And my carefully constructed skepticism began to crumble faster than a poorly optimized web page on my previous device.
Oh, the indignity! The sheer, unadulterated convenience! Suddenly, Samsung Pass isn’t some mythical creature; it’s a thing that actually works! Secure Folder? It exists! Game Booster? My projects are now compiling with the speed of light, and my gaming experience is no longer a slideshow of pixelated despair. The fingerprint sensor actually responds to my touch, like a loyal digital servant, instead of requiring a blood sacrifice and a prayer.
The screen, my friends, is not merely a screen; it’s a window into a universe of vibrant, responsive pixels. The audio, no longer the tinny wail of a dying alley cat, is deep. IP54 rating? Peace of mind? What is this strange magic? It’s lighter. It’s smoother. It has 128 gigs of storage and 4 GB of RAM, which, for a digital hoarder like myself, feels like an infinite expanse. And yes, the absence of an audio jack is yet another sign of my inevitable forced march into modernity, but frankly, I’m too busy compiling code at warp speed to complain.
So here I am, the Architect, the self-proclaimed Technocratic Overlord, confronting a profound philosophical dilemma: Is it acceptable for the self-made titan to accept a leg up when that leg up is precisely what is needed to accelerate the very empire he is building?
My initial, visceral reaction was no. Purity of hustle! Unadulterated self-creation!
My current, pragmatically delighted reaction is: Absolutely.
Because the A05 didn’t fail me; I simply outgrew it. My vision for BradVerse, my projects, my progress—they overwhelmed the very tool that helped me lay the foundation. This A16 isn’t a replacement for hustle; it’s an upgrade to the infrastructure. It’s the next-generation server farm for my digital dominion. It’s the crane brought to the site, not to negate the bricklayer’s skill, but to build taller, faster, more efficiently.
So, while a part of me mourns the loss of that glorious, character-building struggle, the larger, more ambitious part of me—the Architect who thrives on efficiency and forward momentum—is quietly, shamefully, and utterly thrilled.
My mom didn’t just give me a phone; she gave me an accelerant. And for that, even a self-made demigod must occasionally admit: sometimes, a well-timed gift isn’t a sign of weakness, but a catalyst for the next, even grander, phase of conquest.
Now, if you’ll excuse me, I have some applications to compile without freezing, and some worlds to build. And this time, I won’t have to wait five minutes for the prompt. The indignity!
